request: A story about a girl named Alice and her best friend Bob, who happens to be a cat.

first_draft.title: Alice and Bob and the Apple Tree Treasure
first_draft.text:
Alice had a cat named Bob, and Bob had a whiskery nose that twitched every time the kettle began to sing. Bob was orange, the colour of marmalade, and he had a white patch on his chest like a tiny bib. Every morning he sat on the windowsill and watched the garden, and every morning Alice sat beside him with her chin in her hands.

One grey afternoon, Alice noticed that Bob was not watching the garden. He was watching the bookcase. Something small and silver was rolling along the top shelf, going tick, tick, tick, like a clock with a cough.

"What is it, Bob?" whispered Alice.

Bob crouched low, tail flicking, and then he leapt. Thump went his paws on the rug. Clatter went the shelf. Down tumbled a tiny silver key, spinning round and round until it landed with a plink right at Alice's feet.

"A key!" said Alice. "But what does it open?"

Bob sniffed the key. Then he trotted to the wooden box under the window, the one with the brass corners, and sat in front of it with great dignity. He blinked at Alice. He blinked at the box. He did not move one whisker.

Alice tried the key in the lock. It was too small. She tried turning it the other way. It stuck. She tried again, gently, the way Grandma had taught her to coax a stubborn jar. Click. The lid lifted with a sigh, and inside lay a folded map, a red button, and a tangle of old ribbon.

"Oh, Bob," breathed Alice. "It's a treasure map."

Bob purred so loudly that the teacups rattled. He stepped onto the map and pressed one paw down on a little drawn cross, right beside a squiggly line marked GARDEN.

So they went. Alice wore her wellies, which squelched with every step. Bob walked ahead with his tail held high like a flag. They checked under the rhubarb, behind the water butt, and inside the old wheelbarrow, where a surprised hedgehog blinked at them and then rolled away with a grumpy hiccup. At last they reached the apple tree, and there, tucked between two roots, was a tin with a faded picture of a ship on its lid.

Alice held her breath and lifted the lid. Inside were three ginger biscuits, a pinecone shaped like a crown, and a note in wobbly handwriting that said, For whoever finds this: the best treasure is the one you share.

Alice read it twice. Then she broke one biscuit in half and held out the bigger piece. Bob sniffed it, gave a very polite lick, and then crunched the whole thing in one happy bite.

"Greedy," laughed Alice. She gave him the second biscuit too.

The sun was sinking now, pink and soft, and the garden had gone quiet. Alice tucked the crown pinecone into her pocket, and Bob curled himself around her wellies as they walked slowly back to the house. The kettle was cold. The windowsill was empty. The little silver key lay on the map, shining in the last of the light.

Alice climbed into bed and pulled the blanket up to her chin. Bob hopped up beside her, turned three circles, and settled with a long, warm sigh. Outside, the apple tree rustled its leaves. Inside, the clock went tick, tick, tick, softer and softer, until it was only a whisper.

Goodnight, Alice. Goodnight, Bob.

request: Leo and his dog Rocket go on a treasure hunt in the backyard

first_draft.title: Leo and Rocket's Backyard Treasure
first_draft.text:
Leo found the old pirate map tucked inside a biscuit tin under his bed, and it smelled of salt and dust. A wobbly black X was drawn right beside the big oak tree in the backyard. "Treasure!" whispered Leo. His dog Rocket sat up so fast that his ears flapped like sails.

Leo tied his red bandana around his head. He tucked the map into his pocket and grabbed a spade from the shed. Rocket wagged his tail so hard that the gate rattled. "Ahoy, Captain Rocket!" Leo cried. Rocket barked, which meant yes, of course.

The map said to walk ten giant steps from the birdbath. Leo counted out loud. "One, two, three..." His sneakers squished in the wet grass. At step seven, Rocket stopped and sniffed the ground with a loud, snuffly SNORT. Then he trotted to the compost heap and began to dig, sending soil flying over his nose.

"Wait, Rocket!" Leo laughed, but he knelt down to look. Something shiny peeked out from the dirt. It was not gold. It was a rusty tin whistle with a dented lid. Leo blew it. It gave a squeaky toot, and a sleepy hedgehog poked its head out of the fence hole and blinked at them. Leo giggled so hard he had to sit down.

The map had one more clue, faded and smudged. It said, "Where the shadows stretch at dusk, look up." Leo squinted. The sun was sinking low, and the oak tree's long shadow reached across the lawn like a finger. Leo climbed onto the bottom branch, just the way Dad had shown him, and felt along the bark. His fingers found a little wooden box wedged in a knot. Rocket stood below, barking encouragement and wagging his whole back end.

Inside the box was no pile of coins. There was a folded note in Grandma's loopy handwriting: "Treasure for my brave sailor, who always finds the best adventures right at home." Beside the note sat a smooth blue marble and a chocolate coin wrapped in gold foil.

"A real treasure!" Leo said, grinning. Rocket licked the chocolate coin right out of his hand, and they both laughed.

By the time they walked back to the house, the sky had turned the colour of plums. Leo filled his bath, and Rocket curled up on the bath mat, tired and muddy. Leo hung the map on his bedroom wall, next to his lamp.

He pulled up his blanket and tucked the blue marble under his pillow. The house was quiet. Outside, the oak tree rustled softly, and the wind hummed a slow little song. Rocket sighed on the rug beside the bed. Leo's eyes grew heavy, and the stars blinked one by one, like lanterns on a faraway ship. Goodnight, Captain Leo. Goodnight, Rocket. The garden was quiet, and so was the sea of the night.

first_draft.title: Pipkin and the Very Small Flight
first_draft.text:
High on a cliff, where the wind hummed through the grass, there lived a little dragon named Pipkin. Pipkin had green scales, soft as moss, and a tail that curled like a question mark.

Pipkin had wings, big and speckled gold. But Pipkin never flew. Not once.

Every morning the other dragons zoomed past the cliff. Whoosh! Whoosh! "Come up, Pipkin!" they called. "The sky is sparkly today!"

"Maybe tomorrow," said Pipkin, and tucked the wings close.

One windy morning, a small wobbly sound came from the nest. Pipkin's wings went flap, flap, flap, and then stopped. Pipkin's knees went wobble, wobble, wobble.

"What is the matter?" asked Old Grandmother Ember, who had seen a hundred sunrises.

"The ground is far away," whispered Pipkin. "What if I fall down, down, down?"

Grandmother Ember blinked her slow golden eyes. "Hmm," she said. "Let's try something small first."

So Pipkin hopped off the nest. Hop! Plop! Hop! Plop! Pipkin flapped the wings, very softly. Flap, flap. A tiny lift. Then down again. Plop!

"I flew!" Pipkin squeaked. "Only a crumb of a flight, but I flew!"

"Yes, you did," said Grandmother Ember. "Again?"

Pipkin tried again. Flap, flap, flap. Up went Pipkin, over a patch of purple clover. Then a bumpy landing. Oof! Pipkin rolled into a bush and came out with a leaf on the nose.

A bunny in the clover giggled. Pipkin giggled too. "Maybe my landings need practice," said Pipkin, picking the leaf off.

The next morning, the wind was quiet and warm. The other dragons whooshed by again. "Come on, Pipkin!"

Pipkin took a deep breath. In went the breath. Out went the worry. Flap, flap, flap, WHOOSH! Up, up, over the grass, over the bunny, over the river that sparkled like spilled silver.

For one whole, wonderful minute, Pipkin was flying.

Then Pipkin folded the wings and glided, slow and easy, all the way back to the cliff. Plip. Pipkin landed on the soft moss, neat as a feather.

"Did you see?" Pipkin called. "I didn't fall!"

Grandmother Ember smiled a crinkly smile. "I saw."

That evening, the sun slid down behind the hills. The wind grew soft. The river hushed. Pipkin curled up in the nest, tail wrapped round like a warm blanket.

Flap... went one wing, sleepy and slow.

final.title: Pipkin and the Very Small Flight
final.text:
High on a cliff, where the wind hummed through the tall grass, there lived a little dragon named Pipkin. Pipkin had green scales, soft as moss, and a tail that curled like a question mark. Pipkin liked to sniff the salty air and count the clouds as they drifted by.

Pipkin had wings, big and speckled gold. But Pipkin never flew. Not once. Not even a tiny hop-flight.

Every morning the other dragons zoomed past the cliff. Whoosh! Whoosh! Their wings flashed like copper pans in the sun. "Come up, Pipkin!" they called. "The sky is sparkly today!"

"Maybe tomorrow," said Pipkin, and tucked the wings close.

One windy morning, a small wobbly sound came from the nest. Pipkin's wings went flap, flap, flap, and then stopped. Pipkin's knees went wobble, wobble, wobble. Pipkin's tummy went flip, flop, flip.

"What is the matter?" asked Old Grandmother Ember, who had seen a hundred sunrises.

"The ground is far away," whispered Pipkin. "What if I fall down, down, down?"

Grandmother Ember blinked her slow golden eyes. "Hmm," she said. "Let's try something small first. Something as small as a crumb."

So Pipkin hopped off the nest. Hop! Plop! Hop! Plop! Pipkin flapped the wings, very softly. Flap, flap. A tiny lift. Pipkin's feet left the grass for one blink. Then down again. Plop!

"I flew!" Pipkin squeaked. "Only a crumb of a flight, but I flew!"

"Yes, you did," said Grandmother Ember. "Again?"

Pipkin tried again. Flap, flap, flap. Up went Pipkin, over a patch of purple clover, higher than the nest, higher than the tallest blade of grass. Then a bumpy landing. Oof! Pipkin rolled into a bush and came out with a leaf on the nose.

A bunny in the clover giggled. Pipkin giggled too. "Maybe my landings need practice," said Pipkin, picking the leaf off with one claw.

Grandmother Ember said nothing, but her golden eyes crinkled at the corners.

The next morning, the wind was quiet and warm. The other dragons whooshed by again. "Come on, Pipkin!"

Pipkin sat at the edge of the cliff, toes curled over the rocks. Far below, the bunny looked as tiny as a button. Pipkin took a deep breath. In went the breath. Out went the worry. Flap, flap, flap, WHOOSH! Up, up, over the grass, over the bunny, over the river that sparkled like spilled silver.

For one whole, wonderful minute, Pipkin was flying.

Then Pipkin folded the wings and glided, slow and easy, all the way back to the cliff. Plip. Pipkin landed on the soft moss, neat as a feather.

"Did you see?" Pipkin called. "I didn't fall!"

The other dragons cheered and tooted little puffs of silver steam. Grandmother Ember smiled a crinkly smile. "I saw."

That evening, the sun slid down behind the hills. The wind grew soft. The river hushed. Pipkin curled up in the nest, tail wrapped round like a warm blanket.

Flap... went one wing, sleepy and slow.

Hush... went the grass.

Sleep now, little dragon. The sky will still be there in the morning.

first_draft.title: The Midnight Vegetable Party
first_draft.text:
At midnight, when the kitchen clock gave its tiny tick and the moon peeked through the window, the fridge door creaked open by itself. Eight-year-old Nico crept down the hallway in socks, rubbing one sleepy eye. He pressed his nose to the crack of the door and peeked inside.

The carrots were dancing. Round and orange, they hopped in a wobbly line, bumping into each other with soft little thunks. A leek in a striped scarf twirled like a jump rope. Peas rolled across the shelf in a bouncy green crowd, giggling, "Peep, peep, peep!"

"Oh, bother," said a voice from the bottom drawer. It was Mr. Broccoli, who wore a tiny paper crown and looked very worried. "The party needs a music maker, and our drummer has gone missing! Zadie the zucchini has vanished into the vegetable crisper, and we cannot start without her!"

Nico tiptoed to the drawer and peered in. Behind a bag of spinach, he heard a squeaky sound: squeak, squonk, squeak. Nico reached carefully past the leafy greens, and there was Zadie, wedged between two lemons, looking very embarrassed.

"I rolled too far," she whispered, wiggling her long green body. "And now I'm stuck!"

Nico thought hard. He did not pull, because that might bend her. He did not shout, because that would wake Mum. Instead he gently lifted the spinach bag, nudged one lemon to the left with a soft tap, and Zadie slid free with a joyful sproing!

The whole fridge cheered. Mr. Broccoli waved his crown. "Now the party can begin!" The celery played a tune on a row of tiny glass bottles, ting, tang, tong. The mushrooms hummed along. Zadie beat a rhythm on a yogurt tub, boomity-boom, boomity-boom, and the peas wiggled so hard they nearly tipped out of their box.

Then Nico noticed something. A small red pepper sat alone at the back, not dancing, not singing, just staring at the cold white wall.

"Hello," Nico whispered. "Do you want to join in?"

The pepper blinked. "I don't know how to dance," she said quietly. "My feet are too round."

Nico grinned. He took a slice of cucumber and made it into a hat, then wobbled his hips in the most silly way he could think of. The cucumber hat fell over his eyes. Zadie laughed so hard she squeaked, and the pepper giggled too.

"Round feet are the best for wobbling," Nico said, and he held out his hand.

So the pepper wobbled. Then she spun. Then she bounced so high that a cheese wedge clapped its corners together in delight. The party roared on until the moon slid behind a cloud.

Slowly, the music grew softer. The peas yawned. The carrots tucked themselves into a neat orange row. Mr. Broccoli folded his crown and placed it on his head like a blanket.

"Goodnight, Nico," he murmured. "Goodnight, fridge."

Nico tiptoed back up the hallway, one sock at a time. The fridge door clicked softly shut behind him. Upstairs, his pillow was cool and his blanket was warm, and the kitchen hummed a little lullaby all the way to sleep.

Shh now. The party is over. The vegetables are resting. Goodnight.

first_draft.text:
The lighthouse keeper's cat had gone missing, and the whole village of Puddle Cove was looking for her.

Osric was seven and a half, and he was sure he could find anything. He tiptoed along the harbor wall with his yellow raincoat flapping and his flashlight clicking on and off. Click. Click. The gulls squabbled overhead. A crab scuttled sideways past his boots, as if it had somewhere important to be.

"Mrs. Bramble Whisker," Osric called softly. "Here, kitty, kitty."

Nothing answered him but the slap of the waves and the creak of a rowboat tied to the dock.

He sat down on an upturned bucket to think. His little sister Linnea came clomping up the boards in her wellies, holding a squashed sandwich. "Did you check the fish shed?" she asked, a crumb stuck to her chin.

"Twice," said Osric. "Mrs. Bramble Whisker does not like fish shed. It smells of old socks."

"Then she likes socks," said Linnea, very seriously, and she sat down beside him.

Osric frowned. He pictured the cat, round and grey, with one white paw like a sock she had dipped in milk. Cats liked warm places. They liked soft places. They liked places where nobody thought to look.

"The laundry basket," he whispered. "On the washing line!"

They ran up the hill, past the blue gate and the snoring dog, to the line where sheets flapped like sleepy ghosts. Osric lifted a towel. Then a pillowcase. Then a striped sock as long as his arm.

From somewhere underneath came a small, offended sneeze. "Pfft!"

Osric grinned so wide his cheeks hurt. He pulled back the old tartan blanket that had been folded on the bench, and there she was, curled up like a grey doughnut with her white paw tucked under her nose.

"Got you," he whispered.

Mrs. Bramble Whisker opened one green eye, stretched every single toe, and yawned a yawn so big that Linnea giggled into her sandwich.

They carried her home between them, Osric holding her middle and Linnea holding her tail, which the cat did not seem to mind at all. At the lighthouse door, the keeper, Mr. Hollis, threw up his hands and laughed. "Where on earth was she?"

"In the washing," said Linnea proudly. "Clean as a whistle."

"Mostly clean," said Osric, and he looked at the cat's whiskers, which were full of lint.

The sky went pink, then lavender, then the soft blue of a blanket pulled up to the chin. Lights blinked on in the cottages. The bell on the buoy gave one slow, sleepy clang.

Osric walked home with his flashlight switched off, because he did not need it anymore. The stars were coming out one by one, like shy friends arriving at a party.

In his bedroom, he tucked his yellow raincoat over the chair and let his eyes drift shut. Somewhere down the hill, a cat was purring in a lighthouse. Somewhere a gull settled on a rooftop with a soft, round sigh.

Hush now. The waves are slow. The lamp is low.

Goodnight, Puddle Cove.

The gulls squabbled overhead. A crab scuttled sideways past his boots, as if it had somewhere important to be.

"Mrs. Bramble Whisker," Osric called softly. "Here, kitty, kitty."

Nothing answered him but the slap of the waves and the creak of a rowboat tied to the dock.

"Then she likes socks," said Linnea, very seriously, and she sat down beside him.

Osric frowned. He pictured the cat, round and grey, with one white paw like a sock she had dipped in milk. Cats liked warm places. They liked soft places. They liked places where nobody thought to look.

"The washing line," he whispered. "Up the hill!"

Osric grinned so wide his cheeks hurt. He pulled back the old tartan blanket that had been folded on the bench, and there she was, curled up like a grey doughnut with her white paw tucked under her nose.

"Got you," he whispered.

Mrs. Bramble Whisker opened one green eye, stretched every single toe, and yawned a yawn so big that Linnea giggled into her sandwich.

They carried her home between them, Osric holding her middle and Linnea holding her tail, which the cat did not seem to mind at all. At the lighthouse door, the keeper, Mr. Hollis, threw up his hands and laughed. "Where on earth was she?"

"In the washing," said Linnea proudly. "Clean as a whistle."

"Mostly clean," said Osric, and he looked at the cat's whiskers, which were full of lint.

first_draft.title: Edith and the Moonbeam Monster
first_draft.text:
Every night, just as the hall clock struck seven, something under Edith's bed began to rumble. Rumble-grumble. Glorp. Rumble-grumble-glorp.

Edith held her breath and peeked over the edge of her blanket. Two round eyes blinked back at her, glowing green like pond lilies. Then a furry head rose up, then two long arms, then a belly as round as a pumpkin.

“Good evening,” said the monster, in a voice like a kettle just before it sings. “I am Mossgrumble. I am very, very hungry.”

Edith's heart thumped, but not very hard. A monster who said good evening was difficult to be scared of. “What do you like to eat?” she whispered.

“Pancakes first,” said Mossgrumble, licking his lips with a noise like a squeaky gate. “Then moonbeams for pudding. Silvery ones, with a sprinkle of starlight on top.”

Edith tiptoed to the kitchen, with the monster trailing behind her, going pat, pat, pat on his big bare feet. Grandpa Hector sat at the table with his reading glasses on his nose. He looked up, saw the monster, and only said, “Ah. Is he hungry?” Edith nodded. Grandpa slid a plate of cold pancakes across the table and went back to his newspaper, humming softly.

Mossgrumble ate eleven pancakes in one gulp. Glorp! Then he licked up the syrup, then the crumbs, then the plate. “Delicious,” he said, hiccupping small puffs of sparkles. “Now for the pudding.”

Edith went to the window and looked up. The moon was there, round and creamy, but thick white clouds sat in front of it like sleepy cats on a sill. Not one moonbeam was getting through.

“Can you blow the clouds away?” Edith asked.

Mossgrumble puffed out his cheeks and blew. The clouds only wobbled, drifted back, and settled down again, looking pleased with themselves.

Edith tried her torch next. Mossgrumble tasted the beam, screwed up his face, and groaned, “That tastes like a wet sock.”

Then Edith remembered the silver tray on the bottom shelf of the cupboard, the one Grandma used for birthday cakes. It was dusty, so Edith rubbed it with her pyjama sleeve until it shone like a spoon. She carried it to the window, tipped it carefully, and angled it toward a thin gap in the clouds.

A small silver beam jumped off the tray and landed right on the monster's nose.

“Ooooh,” breathed Mossgrumble. “Tickly and cold and fizzy, all at once!” He opened his mouth wide and slurped. Slurp, slurp, slurrrp. The moonbeam wiggled like a silver worm and vanished inside him. His belly glowed, then his ears, then the tips of his toes.

“Edith,” he said, “that is the finest pudding I have ever eaten. Could you do one more?”

Edith held the tray steady, and the clouds, as if they were being polite, drifted off to one side. Another beam spilled across the floor like melted butter.

Grandpa Hector appeared in the doorway, yawning. “Bedtime, you two,” he said softly.

Mossgrumble folded himself back under the bed. His green eyes dimmed, one lantern at a time, until only a faint glow was left. Edith pulled her blanket up to her chin. Outside, the moon slid slowly across the sky, and the clouds wandered home, one by one.

The clock ticked. The house grew quiet. Rumble, went the monster, very softly now. Glorp.

“Goodnight, Mossgrumble,” Edith whispered.

“Mmm… goodnight, Edith,” came the sleepy reply, and then there was only the sound of gentle breathing.

The castle sat on a hill, and the wind blew through its tall grey towers like a whistling kettle. Sir Hamish the Hopeful polished his helmet every morning until it shone like a spoon. Today he had a visitor. A small brown goat named Pudding trotted up the drawbridge, wearing a red ribbon and a very serious face.

"Halt!" called Sir Hamish, lifting his wooden sword. "Who goes there?"

"Pudding goes there," said the goat, and she bowed so low her ribbon touched the ground. Then she bounced forward and butted the knight's shield with a loud BONK.

Sir Hamish wobbled. His helmet slipped sideways over one eye. "A challenge!" he cried, delighted. "Very well, Pudding. A sword fight!"

So they fought. Clink went the wooden swords. Clonk went the shield. The goat leapt left, the knight hopped right, and they both spun in a circle until the courtyard grass was full of bounces. Pudding let out a squeaky bleat that sounded just like a rusty gate, and Sir Hamish laughed so hard he had to sit down on a barrel.

Then his boot caught the edge of a bucket. Splash! Sir Hamish sat in a puddle of muddy water with a bucket on his head.

He was quiet for a moment. Pudding stared at him with her round yellow eyes. Then a small sound came out of the bucket. It was a hiccup, and then another, and then a giggle.

"I am perfectly fine," said Sir Hamish from inside the bucket. "I am a very wet knight, that is all."

Pudding trotted over and nudged the bucket with her nose. It rolled off with a clatter, and there sat the knight, dripping and grinning, with a leaf stuck to his nose.

"Truce?" he asked, holding out his hand.

Pudding considered this. Then she pressed her soft head into his palm. "Mmmeh," she said, which everyone agreed meant yes.

They sat together on the warm stones of the courtyard while the sun slid lower behind the towers. A breeze rustled the apple tree. A owl hooted somewhere far away, hoo, hoo, soft as a sleepy yawn.

Sir Hamish wrapped his cloak around his shoulders and let out a long, slow breath. Pudding curled up against his side, her ribbon tucked under her chin. The stones were still warm. The wind had gone quiet.

"Goodnight, Pudding," whispered the knight.

The goat's eyes closed, one slow blink at a time, and the castle grew still around them.

On Monday morning, Maya had a frog in her tummy. It hopped. It bounced. It went boing, boing, boing.

"Do I have to go?" she asked.

Her mum knelt down and tied Maya's shoelaces in two neat bows. "Your new school is waiting for you," she said. "And I will be right here at the gate."

Maya held her backpack tight. Its yellow tag said MAYA in big, bold letters. It was the one thing she knew for sure.

Inside, the classroom was loud. Chairs scraped. Pencils rattled in tin pots. Somewhere a bell went ding-a-ling.

Maya stood at the door. Her feet felt stuck, like wet socks on a wooden floor.

"Hi," she whispered to a girl with purple socks. The girl was busy and did not look up.

"Hi! I like your socks," Maya tried again. The girl laughed, then turned to talk to someone else. Maya's cheeks went hot and pink.

So Maya sat at the end of a long table, all by herself. She opened her pencil case and drew a sun. Then she drew a cat with a very long tail. The frog hopped again. Boing. Boing.

Across the table, a boy with curly orange hair was doing the same thing. He tapped his pencil. Tap, tap, tap. Then he let out a big, wobbly sigh. "Pffft-oooh."

Maya peeked over. "Is your frog bouncing too?" she asked.

The boy's eyes went wide. "How did you know?"

"I have one too," said Maya. "His name is Boing. He is very bouncy today."

"Mine is called Wobble," said the boy. "I'm Otis."

Maya giggled. It came out as a squeak. Otis giggled too. His came out as a honk.

"Honk!" said Maya. Then they both honked and squeaked until the whole table was laughing.

Then Otis's pencil rolled off the table. Clatter-tap-ting! It rolled under Maya's chair. Maya ducked down and fished it out.

The pencil was green, with teeth marks on the end. "Thank you," said Otis. "Want to draw my cat? He's round and he's called Mr. Pudding."

Maya nodded. She drew Mr. Pudding with a long tail and four fat paws. Otis added whiskers as long as spaghetti.

A girl with purple socks leaned over. "Is that a dragon or a cat?"

"It's a cat with a dragon's tail," said Maya.

"Cool," said the girl. "I'm Lottie. Can I add spots?"

Lottie drew spots. Otis drew a hat. Maya drew a tiny bell on the collar. Ding-a-ling!

At recess, the playground smelled of cut grass and rain. Lottie showed them a game called Hop, Skip, Squeak.

"Hop on one foot, skip to the gate, then squeak like a mouse!" Lottie called.

"Hop, skip, squeak!" chanted Otis. He squeaked so loudly that a pigeon flew off the fence.

"Hop, skip, squeak!" chanted Maya. Her frog was still bouncing, but now it bounced in time with everybody else.

At the gate, Mum waved. Maya ran to her, a little out of breath. "I did a squeak," she said. "And I drew a cat with Lottie and Otis."

That night, Maya's room was dim. The streetlight glowed through the curtains. Her backpack hung on the chair, its yellow tag still shining.

Her mum tucked the blanket up to her chin. "Tell me about your day," she said.

Maya yawned a big, slow yawn. "There was a frog," she murmured. "And a cat with spots. And two friends."

The frog in her tummy was quiet now. Hush. Hush. Sleep.

The streetlight dimmed. The house settled. Somewhere, a clock went tick... tock...

"Goodnight, Maya," her mum whispered.

"Goodnight," whispered Maya, and her eyes closed like two soft doors.

request: Our old dog Biscuit died last week and Sam misses him a lot

first_draft.title: Sam and the Fourteen Socks
first_draft.text:
The gate at the bottom of the garden used to go clink, clink, clink every evening. That was the sound of Biscuit's tag as he trotted up the path to meet Sam, his grey muzzle wagging and his one white sock flashing in the lamplight. Biscuit had died last week. Now the gate stayed still, and Sam kept looking at it anyway.

On Monday Sam kicked his football against the shed. Thwump. Thwump. Nothing came galloping to fetch it. On Tuesday he built a den out of cushions, but the cushions kept sliding into a heap, and Sam kept picturing Biscuit curled in the middle, snoring like a squeaky bagpipe. "It's not fair," he muttered to the cushions. The cushions did not argue.

That evening Mum came out onto the back step with two mugs of hot chocolate. She sat down slowly, the way you do when you don't want to startle anyone. "I miss him too," she said. "Would you like to tell me one of your favourite Biscuit stories?" Sam stared into his mug. Then, without meaning to, he said, "He stole socks."

"Fourteen," Mum said. "Fourteen socks, under the hedge, in the summer." Sam giggled, a wobbly giggle, and then his chin wobbled too. Mum put her arm around him. They sat together and remembered: the way Biscuit barked at the vacuum cleaner, the way he stole the warm spot on the rug before anyone got home, and the way he always found the ball, even when it had rolled under the sofa. Sam's tears came, and then they went, and Mum didn't hurry them.

Inside, Sam fetched a notebook and a pencil with a chewed end. Mum helped him write the title across the top: THE BOOK OF BISCUIT. On the first page he drew a dog with a sock in its mouth, though the sock looked more like a sausage. Underneath he wrote, He came when the gate went clink. Mum read it and squeezed his hand twice.

Next, Sam lifted Biscuit's lead from its hook by the front door. It was red and worn soft, and it smelled faintly of grass and rain. He held it for a long moment. Then he hung it on the hook by the back door, where he would see it every morning on the way out. The lead swung gently and tapped the wood. Clink. Sam smiled a small smile.

The house settled down around them. Downstairs the kettle clicked off. The moon climbed over the garden, silver on the grass, and the gate stood quiet, just as it should be for now. Sam pulled his blanket up to his chin. "Goodnight, Biscuit," he whispered. A breeze stirred the hedge. Somewhere underneath, he thought, one sock was probably still waiting.

The room grew soft and dim. Sam's eyelids grew heavy. Goodnight, Sam.

first_draft.text:
In the tallest oak at the edge of the meadow, an owl named Florentine blinked her round golden eyes. Her feathers were the soft brown of toast. Tonight, her eyes kept drooping shut.

"Hoo," she yawned. "Hoo-hoo. I need a soft, quiet place to sleep." She spread her wings and glided down, whoosh, whoosh, over the silver grass.

A hedgehog snored in a pile of leaves. "Not here," whispered Florentine. "You are far too prickly for a nap." The hedgehog grumbled and rolled over.

She drifted past the pond, where frogs went plip, plop, croak. A sleepy duck tucked its head under its wing. "Not here," sighed Florentine. "Too much splashing." She turned and flew on, slowly, slowly.

Then, from under a dandelion, came a tiny sniffle. Florentine tilted her head. A little mouse named Hector sat shivering in the grass.

"My leaf blanket blew away," he squeaked. "And the wind is so cold, and the night is so big."

Florentine looked at the leaves scattered all around. She gathered them with her feet, one by one, and fluffed them into a pillow as soft as a cloud.

"Climb on," she said. Hector scrambled onto the pillow. Florentine spread one wide wing over him, like a warm roof.

"Hoo," she yawned, a yawn so big it made Hector giggle. "Now the wind cannot find us."

The moon climbed slowly up the sky. The pond grew quiet. The frogs stopped croaking, one by one.

Hector's breath went in, and out, soft as a feather. Florentine's eyes drooped shut, one heavy blink at a time.

Hush now, meadow. Hush now, little mouse. Hoo... hoo... hush.

Goodnight, sleepy owl. Goodnight, tiny friend.

final.title: Florentine's Soft Nest Under the Moon
final.text:
In the tallest oak at the edge of the meadow, an owl named Florentine blinked her round golden eyes. Her feathers were the soft brown of toast. Tonight, her eyes kept drooping shut.

"Hoo," she yawned. "Hoo-hoo. I need a soft, quiet place to sleep." She spread her wings and glided down, whoosh, whoosh, over the silver grass.

A hedgehog snored in a pile of leaves. "Not here," whispered Florentine. "You are far too prickly for a nap." The hedgehog grumbled and rolled over.

She drifted past the pond, where frogs went plip, plop, croak. A sleepy duck tucked its head under its wing. "Not here," sighed Florentine. "Too much splashing." She turned and flew on, slowly, slowly.

Then, from under a dandelion, came a tiny sniffle. Florentine tilted her head. A little mouse named Hector sat shivering in the grass.

"My leaf blanket blew away," he squeaked. "And the wind is so cold, and the night is so big."

Florentine looked at the leaves scattered all around. She gathered them with her feet, one by one, and fluffed them into a pillow as soft as a cloud.

"Climb on," she said. Hector scrambled onto the pillow. Florentine spread one wide wing over him, like a warm roof.

"Hoo," she yawned, a yawn so big it made Hector giggle. "Now the wind cannot find us."

The moon climbed slowly up the sky. The pond grew quiet. The frogs stopped croaking, one by one.

Hector's breath went in, and out, soft as a feather. Florentine's eyes drooped shut, one heavy blink at a time.

Hush now, meadow. Hush now, little mouse. Hoo... hoo... hush.

Goodnight, sleepy owl. Goodnight, tiny friend.

first_draft.title: Zoe and the Humming Crystal Cave
first_draft.text:
Zoe found the cave on the last wet afternoon of summer, behind a curtain of dripping ivy at the bottom of Hollow Hill. The leaves smelled of rain and cold stone. Pebble, her tortoise, rode in the pocket of her yellow raincoat, his wrinkled head poking out like a button that wanted to see the world.

'Just a peek,' Zoe whispered, and she pushed the ivy aside.

The air changed at once. It was cool and sweet, like the inside of a cupboard full of apples. Zoe clicked on her torch. Its beam wobbled across damp walls, and somewhere far away, water went drip, drip, plink.

'Plink,' said Zoe, trying out the new sound. Pebble blinked slowly, as if he agreed.

The cave split into three tunnels, each one darker than the last. Zoe chose the middle one, because it looked the most like an adventure. She had taken only three steps when Pebble wriggled. He squirmed out of her pocket, plopped onto the rocky floor, and trundled off into the left-hand tunnel, flip-flop, flip-flop, his stubby feet scraping the stone.

'Pebble! Wait for me!'

Her torch flickered. Once, twice. Then it glowed weakly, the colour of weak tea.

'Pebble!' called Zoe. The echo bounced back at her, pebble, pebble, pebble, and she could no longer tell which way he had gone.

Zoe pressed her ear to the rock. Scritch. Scratch. Scritch. That was Pebble, she was almost sure. She crept into the left tunnel, ducking under a low ledge, and her raincoat snagged on a spike. She tugged. It held. She tugged again and tore free with a squeak of wet plastic.

'Oops,' she said, and then, more softly, 'Sorry, cave.'

Scritch, scratch. Down a little dip the tunnel turned into a puddle as wide as a bathtub. Zoe stepped in. Splosh! Her sock went soggy and squelchy. Somewhere ahead, Pebble answered with a small sound that might have been a snore or might have been a yawn.

Zoe stopped. Her heart thumped like a rabbit's. Then she did what her grandma always said: stop, breathe, and listen.

In the quiet she heard the drip again, and then something else, a soft humming, like a spoon tapping a glass. Zoe followed it around a bend, and the cave opened into a round room.

Crystals covered every wall. Some were as tall as her dad, and some were as small as her thumb. They glowed lilac and honey and a pale, cool blue, and each one hummed faintly with light. When Zoe's torch touched them, rainbows jumped across the ceiling.

'Oh,' breathed Zoe. 'Oh, Pebble.'

Pebble sat in the middle of the room, right beneath the biggest crystal, looking extremely pleased with himself, as if he had arranged the whole thing.

Zoe knelt beside a fallen crystal, a sparkling purple point no longer than her finger. It would fit perfectly in her pocket. She could almost feel it warm in her palm. Her hand hovered over it.

Then she noticed the tiny pale ridges on the wall, the places where new crystals were still growing. They grew slowly, slowly, like a snail on a long journey. A crystal that took a hundred years to grow ought to stay where it was, so the next visitor could gasp at it too.

Zoe pulled her hand back. 'You stay here,' she whispered to the purple point, and she left it glittering in the dark.

Then she felt it: a cool breath against her cheek. A breeze. Breezes came from outside. Zoe closed her eyes and turned her face towards it. Pebble, who seemed to have a sense of direction after all, began to plod the same way, one slow step at a time. Zoe followed him, one hand on the wall, until grey light spilled across the floor and the ivy rustled ahead.

Dad stood at the entrance with his hands in his pockets and a worried crease between his eyebrows. When he saw her, he crouched down fast.

'I found the most amazing thing,' Zoe said, her voice wobbling. 'But I didn't take it. I left it for the next person to see.'

The crease smoothed out. 'That,' said Dad, 'is the best kind of finding.'

That night, Zoe tucked Pebble into his cardboard box, lined with a soft towel, and switched off her lamp. Her eyes felt heavy. She thought of the purple crystal humming in the dark, and of the rainbows waiting patiently for someone new.

Some wonders are happiest when they stay where they are, growing slowly, so that everyone can find them.

Outside, the rain had stopped. Drip. Plink. Zoe smiled into her pillow.

Goodnight, Pebble.

Goodnight, little crystals.

Shhh.
